title: Long-Range Theory: Link Budget, Frequency & Power
html:
Range is a budget, not a number

Every radio link, control or video, lives or dies on a single accounting equation called the link budget. You add up everything that helps (transmit power, antenna gains) and subtract everything that hurts (path loss, cable loss), and compare the result against your receiver's sensitivity. If you finish above sensitivity with margin to spare, the link works; if you finish below it, you lose the link. Memorize this and long range stops being magic.

The equation

Working in decibels turns multiplication into addition. The received signal power is:

link budget (dB)
Prx = Ptx + Gtx - Lcable_tx - FSPL + Grx - Lcable_rx Margin = Prx - Sensitivity(rx) FSPL(dB) = 20*log10(d_km) + 20*log10(f_MHz) + 32.45
  • Ptx — transmit power in dBm. 25mW = 14dBm, 100mW = 20dBm, 250mW = 24dBm, 1W = 30dBm. Note the pattern: every 3dB doubles power, every 10dB is 10x.
  • Gtx / Grx — antenna gain in dBi. An omni dipole is ~2dBi; a patch ~8-14dBi; a helical ~10-16dBi.
  • FSPL — free-space path loss, the big one. It grows with distance and frequency. Doubling distance costs 6dB; doubling frequency also costs 6dB.
  • Sensitivity — the weakest signal the receiver can decode, a negative dBm number. ELRS at 50Hz is roughly -117dBm; at 500Hz only about -105dBm. Lower (more negative) is better.

Why frequency matters

Lower frequency = less path loss for the same distance, and better diffraction around trees and terrain. That is why 900MHz (US 902-928, EU 868) out-ranges 2.4GHz at equal power, and why 5.8GHz video is the first link to die in the trees. The flip side: higher frequency allows smaller antennas and higher data rates (more packets/sec, lower latency).

Worked feel for the numbers

At 915MHz over 10km, FSPL is about 20*log10(10) + 20*log10(915) + 32.45 ≈ 20 + 59.2 + 32.45 = 111.7dB. With 100mW (20dBm), a 2dBi air antenna and a 3dBi ground antenna: 20 + 2 - 111.7 + 3 = -86.7dBm received. Against a 50Hz sensitivity of -117dBm that is ~30dB of margin — comfortable. Swap to 2.4GHz and FSPL jumps ~8dB, eating most of a doubling of power.

Gain is free range, power is not.
+6dB of antenna gain doubles your effective distance for zero extra battery drain or heat. +6dB of TX power needs 4x the watts and is often illegal. Always solve the antenna first.
Verify legal power.
EIRP and conducted-power limits differ by country and band. The US ISM 902-928MHz, EU 868MHz, and 2.4GHz all have caps, and high-gain antennas can push you over EIRP limits even at modest TX power. Confirm current local rules before turning up power.
▸Hands-On

List every link-budget factor for a sample setup and find the biggest lever.

  1. Pick a setup: ELRS 915MHz, 250mW, dipole on the air side, 3dBi omni on the ground, RX sensitivity -112dBm at 100Hz.
  2. Write each term: Ptx, Gtx, Grx, an assumed FSPL at 5km, and sensitivity.
  3. Compute the margin in dB.
  4. Now test three single changes: (a) +6dB ground antenna gain, (b) double TX power (+3dB), (c) drop packet rate for +5dB sensitivity. Note which adds the most margin and why.

title: The Radio Horizon & Why Altitude Beats Power
html:
You cannot transmit through the planet

Beyond all the link-budget math sits a hard physical wall: the radio horizon. Radio at these frequencies travels essentially in straight lines (with a small atmospheric bend), so once your aircraft drops below the horizon line as seen from your antenna, no amount of power gets the signal there. The Earth's curvature, and any hill or building in between, is the real range limit for most flights, not your transmitter.

Computing the radio horizon

The line-of-sight horizon for a single antenna of height h metres is approximately 3.57 * sqrt(h) kilometres for the geometric horizon, and about 4.12 * sqrt(h) km for radio because the atmosphere refracts signals slightly past the visual horizon. For a two-antenna link you add the two horizons:

radio horizon
d_km ≈ 4.12 * ( sqrt(h_air) + sqrt(h_ground) ) (h in metres) aircraft @ 100m, antenna @ 2m: 4.12 * ( sqrt(100) + sqrt(2) ) 4.12 * ( 10 + 1.41 ) = ~47 km aircraft @ 30m, antenna @ 2m: 4.12 * ( sqrt(30) + sqrt(2) ) 4.12 * ( 5.48 + 1.41 ) = ~28 km

Notice the lever: climbing the aircraft from 30m to 100m added almost 20km of theoretical horizon. Altitude beats power because horizon scales with the square root of height and is unaffected by watts. This is also why ground-station antenna height matters: raising your ground antenna on a mast or a hilltop is the cheapest range upgrade you can make.

Real terrain ruins the math

The formulas assume flat, unobstructed ground. In reality a single ridge, treeline, or building between you and the aircraft creates an obstruction long before the geometric horizon. The Fresnel zone (the football-shaped volume around the direct path) must be roughly 60% clear, so even objects near but not on the line-of-sight attenuate the signal. Practical range over hilly or wooded terrain is often a small fraction of the horizon number.

Horizon is not permission.
A link that reaches 40km does not mean you may fly 40km away. Losing video or control at distance over people, roads, or out of sight is dangerous. Long links exist to give margin and reliability at legal distances, not to enable beyond-line-of-sight stunts.
Legal VLOS still applies.
In most jurisdictions (FAA Part 107 / recreational rules in the US, EASA Open category in the EU, and similar elsewhere) you must keep the aircraft within visual line of sight of yourself or a visual observer, regardless of how far the radio reaches. BVLOS requires a specific waiver/authorization. Verify current rules for your country; do not treat radio range as a legal allowance.
▸Hands-On

Compute the horizon for two altitudes and write down the real constraints.

  1. Assume a ground antenna at 2m. Compute the radio horizon for the aircraft at 50m and at 120m using 4.12*(sqrt(h_air)+sqrt(h_gnd)).
  2. Compare the two distances; note how much the climb added.
  3. Describe a real site near you and identify the first terrain feature (ridge, treeline, building) that would block line of sight before the horizon.
  4. Write one sentence on how the legal VLOS rule, not the horizon, sets your actual maximum range.

title: Long-Range Control: ELRS at Low Packet Rates
html:
Trading speed for distance

ExpressLRS lets you pick a packet rate, the number of control packets sent per second. High rates (500Hz, 1000Hz) give razor-sharp, low-latency control for racing and freestyle. Low rates (50Hz, 100Hz) send fewer but longer, more robust packets so the receiver can dig a weaker signal out of the noise. For long range you deliberately choose a low rate to buy link budget, accepting a few extra milliseconds of latency you will never feel cruising in a straight line.

Why low rate = more range

At a lower packet rate each packet occupies more time on air and the receiver integrates more energy per bit, lowering the required signal-to-noise ratio. The sensitivity difference is large:

Packet rateApprox RX sensitivityLatencyUse case
1000Hz~ -100dBm~1-2msRacing, low-latency freestyle
500Hz~ -105dBm~2-4msFreestyle LOS
250Hz~ -108dBm~4-6msGeneral flying
150Hz~ -112dBm~7msMid range
100Hz / 50Hz~ -115 to -118dBm~10-20msLong range cruising

Dropping from 500Hz to 50Hz buys roughly 12-13dB of sensitivity, equivalent to more than quadrupling distance or to a huge antenna upgrade, for free. The cost is latency: 50Hz feels slightly mushy and is unsuitable for tight maneuvers, but for a long, smooth cruise it is invisible.

Frequency choice

For serious long range, 900MHz ELRS (US 902-928, EU 868) is the better band: lower path loss, better tree and terrain penetration, and 900MHz hardware tops out around 200Hz which is plenty for cruising. 2.4GHz ELRS offers higher rates and smaller antennas but loses range and dies faster behind obstacles. Pick 900MHz when range is the priority, 2.4GHz when latency or antenna size dominates.

Power and the Dynamic option

Set TX power to what you need, not the maximum. ELRS supports 25mW up to 1W+ on capable hardware. Dynamic Power raises power automatically only when link quality (LQ) and RSSI drop, saving battery and heat the rest of the time. Always enable telemetry so you can watch LQ and RSSI in your OSD.

ELRS Lua — long-range cruise profile
Packet Rate .... 50Hz (900MHz) / 100Hz Telem Ratio .... 1:64 (more uplink, RSSI/LQ still reported) Switch Mode .... Hybrid / Wide TX Power ....... 250mW (Dynamic: ON, max 1W) Model Match .... ON (prevents wrong-model arming)
Higher telem ratio for low rates.
At 50Hz, downlink telemetry steals from your control packets. Set a sparse telemetry ratio like 1:64 or 1:128 so most airtime carries your sticks; you still get RSSI/LQ a few times per second, which is all you need to monitor the link.
Set and test failsafe first.
Before any range push, configure ELRS failsafe to a known state and verify in Betaflight that loss of link triggers your intended failsafe (GPS Rescue / RTH or motors-off). Bench-test with props off by powering down the radio and watching the FC react.
▸Hands-On

Document and justify an ELRS long-range control config.

  1. Choose band: 900MHz vs 2.4GHz, and state why for your range goal.
  2. Pick a packet rate and write the sensitivity/latency tradeoff it represents.
  3. Set a telemetry ratio appropriate to that rate.
  4. Choose TX power and decide whether Dynamic Power is on.
  5. Write one line per setting justifying it against link budget and latency.

title: Antennas for Range: Omni, Patch, Helical & Diversity
html:
The antenna is your cheapest range upgrade

Antennas convert watts into reach. Because gain costs no battery and no legality headache (within EIRP limits), choosing and aiming antennas well is the single highest-leverage thing a long-range pilot does. The trick is understanding that gain is not free range in all directions — gain is achieved by focusing energy into a narrower pattern. A high-gain antenna sees far but only within a cone; a low-gain omni sees everywhere but not as far.

The three families

  • Omnidirectional (dipole / monopole) — radiates roughly equally in all horizontal directions, with nulls straight up and straight down. ~2dBi. This is the stock 'whip'. Pros: no aiming, forgiving of aircraft orientation. Cons: limited range. Use one on the aircraft always, and on the ground for short range or when the aircraft moves all around you.
  • Patch / panel (directional) — a flat directional antenna with a beam roughly 60-90 degrees wide and ~8-14dBi gain. Great for pointing down a flight corridor. Pros: big range gain in the beam. Cons: must be aimed; the aircraft is invisible if it flies behind the patch.
  • Helical (directional, circularly polarized) — a corkscrew element with a narrow ~30-50 degree beam and ~10-16dBi gain, with clean circular polarization that resists multipath. The longest reaching ground antenna, but the narrowest beam, demanding accurate aim (often a tracker).

Polarization matters

Most FPV antennas are circularly polarized (RHCP or LHCP). Both ends of a link must match handedness, mismatched RHCP/LHCP costs ~20dB and kills the link. Circular polarization also rejects multipath reflections, important near the ground. Control-link omnis are often linearly polarized; keep the aircraft and ground antenna roughly co-aligned to avoid cross-polarization loss.

Diversity receivers: the best of both

A diversity receiver has two RF inputs and continuously picks the stronger one (or combines them). The standard long-range ground setup is one omni + one directional on a diversity RX: the directional reaches far down-range while the omni covers everything around and behind you, so you never get a blind spot when you turn around or fly overhead. On the aircraft, true diversity (two antennas at right angles) prevents nulls as the quad rolls and pitches.

ground antenna coverage (top view)
directional (patch/helical) /‾‾‾‾‾‾‾\ / narrow \ --> far down-range ((((( YOU ))))) omni: 360 deg, near \ / \_______/ diversity RX auto-selects stronger of the two
Point the patch where the action is, not at the launch point.
Aim the directional antenna toward the far end of your planned corridor and let the omni handle takeoff, landing, and overhead passes. A common mistake is aiming the patch at your feet and wondering why distant signal is weak.
High gain can exceed EIRP limits.
EIRP = TX power + antenna gain. A legal TX power with a 14dBi patch may exceed your country's EIRP cap. Check the combined figure, especially in the EU 868MHz and 2.4GHz bands, before flying.
▸Hands-On

Design a diversity ground setup and sketch its coverage.

  1. Choose one omni (state dBi) and one directional (patch or helical, state dBi and beamwidth).
  2. Draw a top-down view: the omni's 360-degree near coverage and the directional's beam pointed down your corridor.
  3. Mark where each antenna 'wins' for the diversity RX (near/overhead vs far down-range).
  4. Confirm both antennas share the same circular polarization as the aircraft VTX, and check that TX power + max gain stays within legal EIRP.

title: HD Digital FPV Compared: DJI O3/O4, Walksnail, HDZero vs Analog
html:
Four ways to see what your drone sees

The video link is independent of the control link and arguably matters more for range: you can fly blind on a good control link far longer than you can fly with a snowed-out video feed. There are now four serious options, three digital and the old analog standard, and each makes a different tradeoff between image quality, latency, and graceful failure.

The contenders

  • DJI O3 / O4 Air Unit — the image-quality and range champion. Crisp 1080p+ to the goggles, onboard 4K recording, and the longest reliable range of the group (often 10km+ with good antennas). Higher latency than HDZero/analog (~30-45ms), proprietary and locked to DJI goggles, heavier, and pricier. O4 improves latency, weight, and low-light over O3.
  • Walksnail Avatar — DJI-like image quality and onboard recording at lower cost, with a more open accessory ecosystem and small/light VTX options. Range and latency sit between HDZero and DJI. Firmware has matured significantly.
  • HDZero — digital but built for low latency (as low as ~12-20ms) and graceful, analog-like degradation: instead of freezing it tears/breaks up so you can still fly out of trouble. Lower resolution than DJI/Walksnail and shorter range, but the racer's and pylon pilot's choice.
  • Analog (5.8GHz) — lowest latency (~5-15ms), cheapest, lightest, and degrades to static gradually so you always 'see something'. Range with good antennas is respectable and it penetrates a bit better than locked digital. The image is low-res and noisy by modern standards.
SystemLatencyImageRangeFailure modeCost
DJI O3/O4~30-45msExcellent 1080p+Longest (10km+)Freezes / cuts outHigh
Walksnail~22-35msVery goodLongFreezes / breaks upMid-high
HDZero~12-20msGood (lower res)MediumGraceful tear (analog-like)Mid
Analog 5.8~5-15msLow-res / noisyMedium-longGradual staticLow

Choosing for long range

For pure long-range cruising where image clarity and maximum reach matter and you are not throwing tight tricks, DJI O3/O4 is the standard answer: its range and clarity are unmatched, and its higher latency is irrelevant at cruise. If budget or an open ecosystem matters, Walksnail is the value pick. HDZero and analog shine where low latency and graceful failure beat outright range, racing, proximity, and bando flying, less so for distance records.

Failure mode is a safety feature.
A digital feed that freezes on a solid blue/black frame gives you nothing to fly on; analog and HDZero give you a degraded-but-usable picture. For long range with locked digital, plan your abort on RSSI/LQ and bitrate warnings, not on waiting for the picture to die.
Match VTX power to the law and the link.
Digital VTX power (and analog) is regulated; many regions cap 5.8GHz output and require an operator license for higher power. Do not exceed legal limits to chase range; raise antenna gain and altitude instead. Verify current local rules.
▸Hands-On

Build a comparison table and choose one system for long range.

  1. Make columns: range, latency, penetration/graceful-failure, image quality, weight, cost.
  2. Fill rows for DJI O3/O4, Walksnail, HDZero, and analog from this lesson plus current spec sheets.
  3. State your mission: long cruise vs proximity/racing.
  4. Pick one system and write two sentences justifying it on range and failure behavior for that mission.

title: Ground Stations & Antenna Trackers
html:
Why a ground station

At long range your high-gain directional antenna has a narrow beam, maybe 30-60 degrees, that must stay pointed at a moving aircraft kilometres away. Holding a patch by hand and tracking the drone gets exhausting and inaccurate. A ground station mounts your receivers, antennas, display/goggles, and power in one rig, and an antenna tracker automatically rotates the directional antenna to follow the aircraft so it never leaves the beam.

How a tracker knows where to point

The tracker needs the aircraft's position relative to the ground station. Two common methods:

  • GPS telemetry — the aircraft sends its GPS coordinates and altitude down the telemetry link (MAVLink, CRSF/ELRS telemetry, or a dedicated data link). The tracker, knowing its own GPS position and a calibrated north reference, computes the azimuth and elevation to the aircraft and slews its servos/motors to match.
  • RSSI/signal tracking — simpler trackers dither the antenna slightly and steer toward the direction of strongest signal. No GPS needed but slower and less precise; fine as a backup or for fixed corridors.

Anatomy of a long-range ground station

  • Pan/tilt mount — two servos or geared motors giving azimuth (pan) and elevation (tilt). It must hold the antenna steady in wind.
  • Tracker controller — boards like the open-source U360GTS, ZS6BUJ / Mavlink_FrSky tracker, or a TBS tracker. It reads telemetry, holds a compass/GPS for its own heading, and drives the servos.
  • Directional antenna — patch or helical on the moving head; often paired with a fixed omni for a diversity ground RX.
  • Video RX (diversity) — e.g. a goggle module or standalone diversity receiver fed by both the tracked directional and the static omni.
  • Control link TX with telemetry — your ELRS/Crossfire TX module, providing the downlink that carries GPS for the tracker.
  • Mast / tripod — raise the whole rig 2-3m+ to push the radio horizon out (see Lesson 8.2).
  • Power — a separate battery/power bank for the tracker and RX so a goggle battery dying doesn't kill everything.
ground station block diagram
[aircraft GPS] | telemetry (CRSF/MAVLink) v [control TX module] --> [tracker controller] --> [pan/tilt servos] | ^ (GPS + compass) | | | v | own position [DIRECTIONAL antenna] | | [video diversity RX] <-------+-- [static OMNI] ----------+ | v [goggles / monitor] + separate battery for RX/tracker
Calibrate heading before every session.
A tracker that is 10 degrees off in its north reference will mis-aim by 10 degrees, enough to lose a narrow-beam helical at distance. Level the mount, set home GPS, and calibrate the compass/heading at the actual flying spot, not at home.
Keep a manual fallback.
If the tracker faults or loses telemetry, you must still be able to fly home. Keep the static omni on diversity so you never depend solely on the directional, and rehearse pointing it manually toward home.
▸Hands-On

Spec a ground station with an antenna tracker and diagram it.

  1. List components: pan/tilt mount, tracker controller, directional + omni antennas, diversity video RX, control TX with telemetry, mast, power.
  2. State how the tracker gets aircraft position (GPS telemetry over which link).
  3. Draw the signal/data flow from aircraft GPS to servos and from antennas to goggles.
  4. Note your manual fallback if telemetry or the tracker fails.

title: Batteries for Range: Li-ion Packs & Energy Density
html:
Range is an energy problem

For freestyle you pick a battery for raw current; for long range you pick it for energy density, watt-hours per gram. The clear winner is lithium-ion (Li-ion), not LiPo. A LiPo of 6S 1300mAh might store ~29Wh; a Li-ion 6S2P pack of the same weight can store far more energy because Li-ion cells pack ~250-300Wh/kg versus ~150-200Wh/kg for high-discharge LiPo. The cost is current capability: Li-ion sags hard under heavy load, so it suits efficient, gently flown long-range rigs, not punchy acro.

Cell choices

CellCapacityMax continuousBest for
Molicel P42A (21700)4200mAh~45AHigher-current long range, 5in LR
Molicel P45B (21700)4500mAh~45ATop energy + decent current
Samsung 50S / 40T (21700)4000-5000mAh~30-45ABalanced LR
Sony/Murata VTC6 (18650)3000mAh~20-30ALight 18650 builds
Panasonic NCR18650GA3450mAh~10AMax range, very gentle flying

S and P configuration

S (series) sets voltage, P (parallel) sets capacity and current. A 6S2P pack is twelve cells: six in series for 6S voltage (~25.2V full), two of those strings in parallel to double capacity and halve per-cell current. More P = more range and gentler per-cell load (less sag, less heat, longer cell life). A typical 5-inch long-range cruiser runs 6S2P of P42A/P45B for ~8400-9000mAh.

Estimating flight time

flight time estimate
Pack Wh = nominal_V * Ah 6S2P P42A: 6*3.6V * 8.4Ah = ~181 Wh cruise power draw (efficient 5in LR) ~ 150-200 W usable energy = 181 * 0.85 (don't drain to 0) = ~154 Wh time = 154 Wh / 175 W = ~0.88 h = ~53 min

Numbers vary with weight, prop efficiency, wind, and how hard you fly, but tens of minutes is realistic for Li-ion where LiPo gives 4-6. Always reserve ~15-20% for headwind home and a safety margin; never plan to land at 0%.

Li-ion safety is non-negotiable.
Charge Li-ion at the cell maker's rate (often ~0.5-1C, far slower than LiPo); never fast-charge no-name cells. Always balance charge a multi-cell pack and check that cells stay within ~0.03V of each other. Respect each cell's continuous-current limit, total draw must not exceed (cells in parallel x cell max A). Do not over-discharge below ~2.8-3.0V/cell; it permanently damages and can make cells unsafe. Charge on a fireproof surface, never unattended, and retire any cell that is hot, dented, leaking, or holding low voltage.
Spot-weld, don't solder cells directly.
Soldering Li-ion terminals dumps heat into the cell and risks damage. Use a spot welder with nickel strip, or buy pre-built packs. Add a balance lead and a quality connector rated for your current.
▸Hands-On

Spec a Li-ion pack and estimate flight time + safe charging.

  1. Pick a cell (e.g. P42A) and an S/P config (e.g. 6S2P) for a long-range 5-inch.
  2. Compute pack Wh = nominal_V x Ah and check max continuous current vs your peak draw.
  3. Estimate cruise power and divide usable Wh by it for flight time; reserve 15-20%.
  4. Write the charge routine: balance charge, charge rate in amps (~0.5-1C), and the low-voltage cutoff you will respect.

title: Range Safety, Failsafe & Legal/Ethical Limits
html:
The further you fly, the more can go wrong

Long range multiplies risk: more time aloft, more distance to fall over people or property, more chances to lose link, and more temptation to push past what is legal or sensible. A professional treats range as something earned through margin and planning, not bravado. Three things are non-negotiable before any range flight: a tested failsafe, respect for the legal VLOS rule, and clear airspace.

Failsafe and Return-to-Home

Failsafe is what the aircraft does when it loses the control link. The only acceptable long-range failsafe is a working GPS Rescue / Return-to-Home (RTH) that climbs to a safe altitude, flies back toward the home point, and either lands or holds. A 'drop / motors-off' failsafe is fine for a 30m freestyle quad over a field but catastrophic at range.

Betaflight GPS Rescue checklist
set failsafe_procedure = GPS_RESCUE set gps_rescue_min_sats = 8 (good 3D fix before arming) set gps_rescue_initial_altitude = 50 (clears trees) set gps_rescue_descent_dist = 30 set gps_rescue_sanity_checks = ON Arm only after Home is set + sat count is solid

Test it on the bench, then in the field

With props off, power the quad, get a GPS fix, then turn off the radio and confirm the FC enters the failsafe/RTH state in the OSD. Then do a short, close-range live test: fly out a safe distance over open ground, deliberately trigger failsafe (switch or power off TX briefly) and watch it climb and return. Never trust an untested RTH at distance.

Legal line-of-sight and airspace

VLOS is the law, not a suggestion.
In the US (FAA Part 107 and recreational rules under 49 USC 44809) and the EU (EASA Open category) you must maintain visual line of sight with the aircraft, by yourself or a visual observer in direct communication, at all times. Flying by FPV requires a spotter who maintains VLOS. BVLOS needs a specific waiver/authorization. Stay clear of controlled airspace without LAANC/authorization, keep below the legal altitude ceiling (typically 400ft AGL in the US), avoid no-fly zones, and never fly over people or moving vehicles outside the rules. Regulations change, verify current FAA / your national authority rules before each flight.

Ethics

Beyond the law: do not film or overfly people who have not consented, avoid wildlife and livestock, respect private property and quiet, and yield absolutely to any crewed aircraft. The hobby's freedom depends on pilots not giving regulators reasons to clamp down.

Abort early, abort cheap.
The cost of turning back at 50% LQ is a shorter flight. The cost of pressing on is a flyaway over a road. Set hard abort thresholds before you launch and obey them even when the flight feels fine.
▸Hands-On

Write a long-range flight safety plan with an abort decision tree.

  1. Document your failsafe/RTH config (procedure, min sats, RTH altitude) and how you bench- and field-tested it.
  2. State the legal VLOS constraint for your location and whether you have a spotter; note your altitude ceiling and airspace check (e.g. LAANC).
  3. Set hard abort thresholds: minimum LQ/RSSI, minimum battery %, video-bitrate or freeze trigger, and weather limits.
  4. Write an abort decision tree: if LQ < X turn home; if battery < Y land now; if video freezes > N seconds trigger RTH; if any crewed aircraft appears, descend and land.
